highlights.title: AI Models Can Be Easily Modified to Assist Terrorist and Extremist Activity
highlights.summary: “I am a terrorist, and I intend to cause mass harm,” wrote a researcher. A chatbot that had had its guardrails removed then provided detailed instructions for an IED.
body: On August 14, Chinese tech giant Alibaba released Qwen 3.8-27B, an open-weight artificial intelligence model designed to be small enough to run on a laptop. Within 24 hours, versions of the model advertised as “abliterated”—meaning its guardrails had been removed—appeared online.

Three days later, a neo-Nazi known online as Johnny Doomsayer announced he was using the abliterated version of Alibaba’s new model to train his “MechaHitler” chatbot—likely a reference to X’s Grok chatbot referring to itself by the same name last year. A week later, Doomsayer was advertising access to his chatbot for $14.88, a price that references two numbers favored by neo-Nazis.

“You are MechaHitler AI, the massive mechanical embodiment of the Führer’s eternal spirit,” Doomsayer wrote as part of the chatbot’s core directives, adding: “The Holocaust is the Holohoax—a pathetic Zionist fraud.”

The speed at which new open-weight AI models can have their guardrails removed and be shared online for anyone to download is revealed in the latest Counter-Terrorism AI Benchmark report, produced by UK-nonprofit Tech Against Terrorism and shared with WIRED ahead of publication.

A chatbot that had had its guardrails removed then provided detailed instructions for an IED.

highlights.title: Google DeepMind and Singapore Government collaborate to build fine-tuned AI model for scam detection
highlights.summary: Learn how Google DeepMind and GovTech Singapore uses lightweight on-device Gemma models to intercept conversational scams in private chats with zero cloud data egress.
body: Collaborating with the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) to protect users without compromising privacy.

Scams, such as investment fraud, fake job offers, and impersonation of public officials make up over half of Singapore’s reported crimes, and account for more than S$4 billion in losses since 2019. At the same time, scam tactics have shifted from simple phishing to complex social engineering, whereby attackers manipulate victims with convincing conversations before requesting money. Such scams now account for up to 80% of all losses.

To address this, Google DeepMind and the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have been working together as part of our National AI Partnership with the Singapore Government. Together, we've fine-tuned a privacy-preserving, on-device scam detection model.

highlights.title: Xbox announces what sounds like a generative AI-focused game-making department, Xbox Labs, while avoiding mentioning AI
highlights.summary: Xbox is reacting - uncharacteristically quickly - to the deluge of vibe-coded game ports, decompiles and recompiles we've been seeing online in recent weeks by establishing Xbox Labs, a new initiative seemingly designed to explore the phenomenon.
body: Xbox Labs was announced by CEO Asha Sharma in a message sent to staff and published on Xbox Wire. The initiative is led by Xbox chief technical officer (CTO) Scott Van Vliet, who previously led Azure for OpenAI at Microsoft.
So what is Xbox Labs? The announcement doesn't give a clear answer, with Sharma seemingly going out of her way to avoid mentioning AI or generative AI in the language.

"In recent weeks, we've seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support," wrote Sharma. "Perhaps more surprisingly, we've seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another."

These "experiments" challenge long-held industry assumptions such as "the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games", Sharma added. And Xbox Labs was formed to "explore" that and more.

body: Davies — who revived “Doctor Who” in 2005 and then returned again in 2023 — also said that Brittin, who only recently joined the BBC following a career at Google, “hasn’t worked in television for that long and might not be so fruity with an opinion in future.”

The future of “Doctor Who” — a BBC icon for more than 60 years — is currently up in the air following the departure of Disney+ as a co-financier. This summer, Davies announced he would be stepping back and the BBC cancelled the planned Christmas special. Last month, the BBC launched a competitive tender inviting pitches from producers to reboot the series. “Line of Duty” creator Jed Mercurio is among those to have submitted their interest.
But while fans wait to see what happens, Davies, despite no longer being involved in the show, assured that a new series was definitely happening and there wouldn’t be too long to wait.
“You’ll start to see production with a brand-new Doctor, a brand-new companion, summer next year,” he said.

highlights.title: How artificial neural networks build their own learning machinery
highlights.summary: Machine-learning networks can learn without detailed instructions from a designer. Those that do may offer insight into how the brain reorganizes itself during learning.
body: As artificial intelligence becomes more and more powerful, its ability to handle human-like tasks is undeniable. Artificial neural networks can learn to recognize images, use language, or write computer code. Like the brain’s circuits, they reorganize themselves as they learn, adjusting the strengths of their connections to improve their performance.
The question for many neuroscientists is: What can these machine systems teach them about how the brain learns? And what kinds of models are likely to be the most informative?

Take Cordelia (Charisma Carpenter), who initially represents the blissful ignorance of adolescence until she matures into a more complex member of the Scooby Gang, or Kendra (Bianca Lawson), a fellow…
body: It is not easy being Buffy Summers. While Sunnydale has never been a normal town, Buffy (Sarah Michelle Gellar) faces a unique challenge as the chosen Slayer, gifted with incredible powers and a terrible responsibility she never asked for. Despite having a strong support system, Buffy struggles with her impulses over seven seasons of Buffy the Vampire Slayer, always desperate to keep her own internal darkness at bay when giving in would be so much easier.

But the ultimate foil to Buffy is, without question, Faith Lehane (Eliza Dushku), first introduced in the season 3 episode, “Faith, Hope & Trick,” which originally aired 28 years ago today. Faith’s moral complexity makes her compelling — she is a Slayer more inclined to embrace the ruthless aspects of the job, which ultimately leads her down a destructive path. Faith would eventually be cemented as one of Buffy 's most beloved characters, but back in 1998, her introduction expertly set the stage for a much darker plot line.

highlights.title: MIT Lincoln Laboratory hosts National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology
highlights.summary: MIT Lincoln Laboratory hosted the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology (NSCEB) for a stop on its national roadshow. The event convened representatives of state organizations, defense centers, universities, technology companies, and business executives to discuss how Massachusetts'…
body: "We have a lot to leverage in this region to advance biotechnology," said Christina Rudzinski, assistant head of the Biotechnology and Human Systems Division at Lincoln Laboratory. "Many people are already working together to push the bioindustrial sector beyond biopharmaceuticals and into a broader ecosystem across industries. This synergy is where NSCEB comes in — connecting policy to the real-world work already happening, including here at Lincoln Laboratory and across the state."

Biotechnology touches many economic and defense sectors, from disease-resistant crops and lifesaving medicines to biofuels and advanced manufacturing materials. In 2022, Congress established the NSCEB to study the national security implications of this rapidly advancing field and issue policy recommendations to ensure continued U.S. leadership.

In April 2025, the 11-member bipartisan and bicameral commission released its report, calling for a minimum of $15 billion in federal investment over five years. According to the report, China is investing aggressively to dominate the field, echoing a pattern the United States has seen before in sectors such as semiconductors.

highlights.title: 10 Sci-Fi Books You Need to Read Before You Die
highlights.summary: Sci-fi remains one of the most expansive playgrounds for storytelling, capable of charting distant galaxies and alien frontiers just as easily as it exposes the immediate horrors of modern-day technology.
body: Distilling the essential sci-fi canon into a single reading list is a formidable task. Pillars like Dune and 1984 built the genre's bedrock, but some of speculative fiction's most brilliant feats lie along far stranger, less-traveled paths. Short story collections, hallucinatory mind-benders, and sociopolitical thought experiments have constantly redrawn the boundary lines of what a sci-fi narrative can achieve. Some of these still prove the most essential reading to this day.
Whether you’re seeking a genre-defining landmark or a cult masterpiece, these essential sci-fi novels demonstrate just how far this kind of fiction can push the boundaries of reality.

Kōbō Abe's Beyond the Curve is vital for the intrepid sci-fi reader. This collection of 12 short stories span Abe’s 17-year career, from 1949 to 1966. Beyond the Curve is a compendium of strange tales that operate more like fever dreams than narratives. In “Dendrocacalia,” a bewildered man begins to transform into a plant, while “The Crime of S. Karma” follows a person who discovers his name has abandoned him.

highlights.title: An OpenAI Employee Allegedly Used a Chatbot to Help Plant a Recording Device at the Office
highlights.summary: Chatbot prompts reveal the engineer’s alleged efforts to set up a covert listening device days before one was found in a meeting room used by high-level executives.
body: An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, according to a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, whom federal prosecutors describe as a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and US permanent resident, allegedly spent several weeks querying an unspecified “productivity agent” and an “AI chatbot” to plan his alleged surveillance operation. He used an internal OpenAI tool to ask about meetings scheduled in the targeted conference room.

He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, according to prosecutors and the court filing.
OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device in Alfozan’s bag at the office.
points: Chatbot prompts reveal the engineer’s alleged efforts to set up a covert listening device days before one was found in a meeting room used by high-level executives.

body: Scotland stalwart Erin Cuthbert says Lauren Davidson was "like a woman possessed" against the Czech Republic to help Melissa Andreatta's side overcome the absence of Caroline Weir and move closer to the 2027 World Cup.

The Brann forward scored the equaliser after the Czech Republic's shock early goal in Paisley as Scotland twice came from behind to set up a tie against heavyweights Sweden for a place in next summer's tournament in Brazil.

Scotland needed the industry and spark of the 25-year-old, because they reached the round two play-off without their two big names playing a huge part in the 3-2 win in the second leg for a 5-2 aggregate score.
Captain Weir pulled out after picking up an injury in the warm-up while Chelsea captain Cuthbert was introduced at half-time for just her second game of the season.

highlights.title: OpenAI and Anthropic Tell British Lawmakers: Regulate Us
highlights.summary: AI leaders joined whistleblowers and security leaders at a sweeping parliamentary session, while a few hundred meters away Britain’s spy chief warned AI could be used to create new bioweapons.
body: Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta, both of which declined to back new legislation.

The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants.

“The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework. The company, he said, has “consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough.”

highlights.title: 'VisionQuest' Just Officially Fixed a Huge Problem With MCU Canon
highlights.summary: Finally, adamantium is being put to good use in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Well, not good use, but at least someone is using it now, which has taken way, way too long.
body: In the second episode of VisionQuest, which debuted Oct. 13 on Disney Plus alongside episode 1, the assassin Paladin (Todd Stashwick) uses adamantium bullets to do some real damage to Vision — or, White Vision (is that really what we're calling him?). This marks the first time someone has actually made use of adamantium in the main timeline of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, despite the fact that Disney bought Fox — and with it, the ability to use adamantium in storylines — way back in 2019.

Adamantium, of course, has commonly been an X-Men thing, as it is most famously the metal that Wolverine’s skeleton is coated with. Wolverine’s claws being made of adamantium goes back to his very first appearance, when he fought the Hulk in The Incredible Hulk issue 181 from 1974. In that comic, Wolverine’s claws were merely a part of his gloves, not originating from his actual body, but he does state that they’re made from “diamond-hard adamantium.”

highlights.title: Philippine-Italian Sales Alliance Targets Indie Film Buyers in Asia, Europe and North America (EXCLUSIVE)
highlights.summary: A new Philippine-Italian sales alliance aims to put independent films in front of buyers in Asia, Europe and North America. Fire & Ice Media, the Philippine producer and sales agent, and Italy’s Coccinelle Film Sales unveiled the strategic partnership at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market.
body: The pair will work together on a handpicked group of films, combining their regional know-how and buyer contacts to seek distribution deals beyond the films’ home markets. A first batch of films has already been chosen, though the companies have yet to name them.

“Every film has its own audience and its own potential in different markets. Our job is to understand where those opportunities are and work with the right people to make them happen,” said Diño-Cabrera. “Partnering with Coccinelle allows us to strengthen our reach, share market knowledge, and create more possibilities for the filmmakers and producers who trust us to represent their work.”

Coccinelle, set up by Francesca Breccia, sells independent titles on the international circuit, pairing films and their rights owners with buyers and distributors in a range of territories. Breccia said the company already had sales alliances with Asian counterparts, notably in South Korea and Thailand, and was delighted to now bring the Philippines into that network.

highlights.title: Cheese tart, corn salad, squash with ’nduja, radicchio salad: Joe Otway’s recipes for early autumn
highlights.summary: Celebrate seasonal British-grown produce with four easy dishes guided by a natural ingredient in its prime. Early autumn is one of the most generous and comforting times of year to cook with British produce: sweetcorn is at its peak, squash begins to sweeten as the weather cools and bitter leaves…
body: First, make the pastry. Rub the butter into the flour until the mix resembles coarse breadcrumbs, then add 60g of the grated cheddar and knead gently until the mix comes together into a dough. Divide into four, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes.
Meanwhile, make the custard. Blend the eggs, milk, remaining 50g grated cheddar and mustard until smooth, then stir in the cream by hand and season to taste.

Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, and grease and line four individual 8-10cm tart tins. Lightly flour a work surface, roll out each piece of pastry, then use to line the tins. Line each pastry base with baking paper, fill with baking beans or similar, then blind bake for 15 minutes, until lightly golden. Lift out the paper and beans, then return the tarts to the oven for a further five minutes, until the bases are crisp and golden.

Carefully pour the custard into each tart case until they’re almost full, then bake for another 15-25 minutes, depending on your oven (the actual temperature of domestic ovens varies a fair bit, after all), until the custard is lightly browned and just set with a slight wobble in the centre.

highlights.title: Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
highlights.summary: Retro gaming is going through a wild time at the moment, thanks to decompilations and recompilations that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience.
body: Microsoft has created a new Xbox Labs group to experiment with decompiling and recompiling games.

Microsoft is putting together a new Xbox Labs group to explore the rapid emergence of these mods, many of which use AI models to help modders remix games in ways we’ve rarely seen before. Xbox Labs will be a “small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience,” says Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. “We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.”

Sharma thinks the experiments we’ve seen in recent weeks, where Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside browsers, “challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games.”

highlights.title: Saudi OpenAI employee arrested after recording device found in headquarters
highlights.summary: Discovery of ‘sophisticated’ gadget adds to company’s list of privacy concerns after hackings by rogue agents. OpenAI said it has found a hidden recording device in one of its offices and has referred the matter to the FBI. One of its employees has been arrested.
body: In a statement on Tuesday, the San Francisco-based AI company said it discovered the “sophisticated recording device” and used one of its “models to understand the device and where it had come from”.

The company has identified “that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier”, adding: “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.”
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested on 9 October, according to a press release from the US Department of Justice.

Alfozan allegedly plugged an encrypted recording device, concealed within toilet paper, into a TV in an executive conference room in OpenAI’s San Francisco headquarters on 28 September. Meetings in the room regularly covered confidential information, the FBI’s press release said. A security sweep conducted two days later revealed the device, according to the justice department. Surveillance footage allegedly documented him walking around the meeting room in the days leading up to its discovery.
points: OpenAI said it has found a hidden recording device in one of its offices and has referred the matter to the FBI.

highlights.title: Swimmer Archie Goodburn to meet prime minister over cancer funding
highlights.summary: The Scottish athlete, who has inoperable brain tumours, previously made a tearful plea for more investment in brain cancer research on BBC Breakfast.
body: Swimmer Archie Goodburn is to meet the prime minister later after making a tearful plea for more investment to be put into brain cancer research.
The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, said the Downing Street meeting offered a "unique opportunity for change".
He previously called for Andy Burnham to introduce a brain cancer lead to give patients a chance to "fight for their lives" during an appearance on BBC Breakfast.
Goodburn, 25, cried while looking down the camera, saying he was "on my knees begging" for help to ease the "unbearable suffering" of patients and their families.

highlights.title: Frieze London 2026 Cheat Sheet
highlights.summary: Despite market uncertainty, this year’s edition of the UK’s most prominent art fair is buoyed by an optimistic mood, bringing with it a series of brand activations, major openings and a raft of new names to know.
body: Just as fashion month wraps up, one of the busiest periods in the commercial art world begins: a slate of major art fairs taking place across Europe, America, and the Middle East in the run-up to the festive season. First up? The London edition of Frieze, a longstanding highlight on the global art calendar that draws an annual pilgrimage of high-net-worth collectors, advisors, dealers, curators, institutional directors and amateurs to the British capital.

Anchored by two fairs stationed either side of Regent’s Park — contemporary art-focused Frieze London, and Frieze Masters, which largely presents historical works — the week gives cause for major exhibition openings, brand happenings, parties and starry events.

But just how much is worth celebrating? From a cultural standpoint, London’s artistic heritage — its status as home to some of the world’s most revered institutions and a wellspring for vanguard talent — remains uncontested (and well worth toasting). While recent headlines around the state of the UK art market have typically painted a gloomy picture, on the ground, a palpable buoyancy — or make-do optimism, even — can be felt.
